title: The Dog's Buddha-Nature
author: Zhanran
excerpt: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature too?" This is a very famous koan of the Chan school. It is famous because the Zen master Huangbo of the Tang dynasty, in his Essentials of the Transmission of Mind, used this koan to open the way to the practice of huatou meditation.

inline.s: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature too?" This is a very famous koan of the Chan school. It is famous because the Chan patriarch Huangbo of the Tang dynasty, in his Essentials of the Transmission of Mind, used this koan to open the way to the practice of huatou meditation.

[Pioneer (xian he, 'first river')] The Record of Rites, chapter 'The Record of Learning,' says: 'When the three kings sacrificed to the rivers, they first sacrificed to the river and afterward to the sea.' The ancients regarded the Yellow River as the source of the sea; when the emperors sacrificed, they first offered to the Yellow River and then to the sea. Later, 'first river' was used to refer to the one who was the first to initiate a thing.
The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says:

"If you are a true man, look into a koan. A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said: 'Wu (no).' Simply go, throughout the twelve periods of the day, concentrate upon the word 'wu' — in daytime meditation and nighttime meditation, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether putting on clothes or eating, whether relieving yourself, keep your mind ever on it, and rouse yourself with great vigor
(gathering up your spirit)

to hold fast to the word 'wu.' As days grow long and months deepen, all becomes one mass; suddenly the flower of your mind bursts open, you awaken to the essential activity of the Buddhas and the patriarchs, and you can no longer be fooled by the tongues of the old masters of the world. You will then open your big mouth: 'Bodhidharma came from the West, raising waves where there was no wind; the World-Honoured One held up a flower — one great blunder.' Having reached this point, what matter is King Yama? Even a thousand sages can do nothing to you! Do you not believe that it is truly this
(such)

wonderful? Why is it so? Because deeds fear a determined mind! A verse says: 'Transcending the dusty toils is no common feat; grip the nose-rope and make the whole battle complete. Were it not that one winter chills you to the bone, how should the plum blossom's scent reach your nose alone.'"

[Vigor (jingcai)] Here it means 'spirit.' [Dusty toils (chenlao)] The mind toiling amid the dust of the objects of sense, a name for affliction. [Grip the nose-rope and make a battle] This uses herding cattle as a metaphor: tightly hold the nose-rope by which the mind-cattle is herded, and that nose-rope is the huatou, the word 'wu.' The moment the huatou is lost, the mind-cattle rushes wildly, even eating the crops (a metaphor for doing evil), and so one must 'grip the nose-rope and make a battle.'
By the Song dynasty, the great master Dahui ardently promoted the practice of huatou meditation. Though huatou come in many kinds, he especially encouraged holding up the single word 'wu.'
Dahui says:

"A thousand doubts, ten thousand doubts — in the end but one doubt. Once the doubt on the huatou is broken, then ten thousand doubts dissolve in a single moment; but if the huatou is not broken, then stay with it and grapple
(wrestle with it)

right there upon it. If you abandon the huatou and instead raise doubt on other words, raise doubt on the sutras and treatises, raise doubt on the koans of the ancients, or raise doubt amid the daily toils of life, all these are companions of the evil one. Above all, you must not seize upon the point where it is raised, nor must you speculate and reckon, but simply turn your attention to that which cannot be thought about, while the mind has nowhere to go. Like a rat entering a cow's horn
(it can only go forward, never retreat)
, then you will see the decisive break
(you will see the outcome, that is, see the mind and realize the nature)

. Again, if your heart is disturbed, just hold up the koan of the dog's lack of Buddha-nature. The words of the Buddhas, the words of the patriarchs, the words of the old masters in every quarter — a thousand differences, ten thousand distinctions — if you penetrate the single word 'wu', in one stroke they are all penetrated
(at once all are passed through)
. No need to ask others
(no need to ask anyone)
; if you always
(if you are always)
asking others — what of the Buddha's words, what of the patriarchs' words, what of the old masters' words? — in age after age you will never reach enlightenment."
(From the Record of the Master Dahui Pujue)

[But simply turn your attention to that which cannot be thought about] The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, in 'The Chapter on Yaoshan Weiyan,' records: 'A monk asked: "What do you think of, diligently and without rest?" The master said: "I think of the unthinkable." The monk said: "How does one think of the unthinkable?" The master said: "Non-thinking."' [Old masters (laosu)] Elders of many years and much seniority. In the Chan school the term refers to the mature and venerable ones.
He also says:
"This single
(wu)

word is the very knife that cuts off the road of life and death. When a false thought arises, simply raise the word 'wu'; raise it again and again, until suddenly the trail breaks off — there is the place of finding peace and sitting still at home."
He also says:
"Since you study this Way
(Chan practice)
, throughout the twelve hours, wherever you meet things and respond to conditions, you must not let evil thoughts
(for one practising meditation, anything that is not right mindfulness is an evil thought)
continue in succession. If you fail to watch over yourself and an evil thought arises, you should at once gather your vigor, turn your head sharply
(exchange the thought for the huatou)

. If you simply follow it on and on without interruption, not only does it obstruct the Way, but you are also called a man without wisdom. Formerly Guishan asked Lăn'an: 'Throughout the twelve hours, what is your task?'
(in the twenty-four hours, what are you doing?)
Lăn'an said: 'Herding cattle.' Guishan said: 'How do you herd them?'
(how do you herd?)
Lăn'an said: 'Whenever it goes off into the grass, I seize its nose and drag it back.'
(as soon as the bull leaves the right path, one yanks the nose-rope and drags it back. The meaning is: the moment a false thought arises, one gathers the spirit and raises the huatou.)
'Guishan said: 'You
(you)
truly herd cattle!'
(you are truly herding the mind-cattle!)
The one who studies the Way should restrain
(check)
evil thoughts as Lăn'an herded cattle; then after a long time they will naturally become pure and mature
(false thoughts no longer arise)
(From the Record of the Master Dahui Pujue)
[Lăn'an]

The Zen master Da'an of Changqing in Fuzhou, styled Lăn'an, was of the Chen clan of the prefecture. He received his training on Mount Huangbo and studied the Vinaya. Once he thought to himself: 'Though I labor diligently, I have not yet heard the profound and ultimate principle.' So he left alone, staff in hand, on pilgrimage. As he was about to go to Hongjing and pass by Shangyuan, he met an old man who said to him: 'If you go to Nanchang, you will attain something.' The master then went to Baizhang, bowed, and asked: 'This student wishes to recognize the Buddha — what then is it?' Baizhang said: 'It is very much like riding an ox in search of an ox.' Lăn'an said: 'After recognizing it, what then?' Baizhang said: 'It is like a man riding the ox home.' Lăn'an said: 'I do not understand how to guard and maintain it from beginning to end.' Baizhang said: 'Like a cowherd who, holding his staff, watches it and does not let it trample the crops.' From then on the master grasped the purport and no longer rushed about in pursuit. His fellow practitioner, the Venerable You of the same school, went to found a seat on Mount Guishan, and the master himself worked the fields to assist the Way. When You passed away, the assembly asked the master to take up the abbotship in turn. Mounting the hall he said: 'All of you have come to rely upon me (all of you have come to take refuge with me) — seeking what? If you wish to be a Buddha, you are already a Buddha yourselves. Carrying a Buddha on your back and running around other homes, like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage, when will you ever find accord! If you wish to be a Buddha, simply put away the many inversions, clingings, vain imaginings, evil perceptions, and defilements; the mind of sentient beings is itself the Buddha of the original thought and right awakening — where else would you seek it! For thirty years here at Guishan I have eaten Guishan's rice, voided Guishan's dung, and never learned Guishan's Chan. I merely watch a single water-buffalo; if it strays from the road into the grass, I seize its nose and drag it back; the moment it tramples the crops, I drive it and tame it. After long, pitiable enough, it is receptive to human words; now it has become a white ox in the open air, always present before me, all day clearly and plainly staying close, unable to be driven away
(all day long it stands clearly and unmistakably before one, impossible to chase away)
." (From the Chan Grove and Jade Forest Annotations)
[Mirage (yang yan)]

A kind of vapor produced under a scorching sun; seen from afar it looks like water, so the thirsty long to drink it, yet it can never be obtained. It is used as a metaphor for illusions. It is one of the ten similes of the Great Vehicle.
[White ox in the open air]
The 'open air' is the vacant ground outside the gate, a metaphor for a place of safety and peace; the 'white ox' signifies a pure ox. In the Parable chapter of the Lotus Sutra
the white ox is used as a simile for the One Vehicle teaching, and thus the pure realm free of the least defilement of affliction is called the white ox in the open air.
The Gateless Barrier says:

"To sit in meditation one must pass the barrier of the patriarchs; to attain wondrous awakening one must exhaust the path of the mind. If the barrier of the patriarchs is not passed, if the path of the mind is not exhausted, then all are but spirits clinging to grass and attached to trees. Now tell me: what is the barrier of the patriarchs? Just this
(this)

single word 'wu' is a barrier of the school. Hence it is called the ungated barrier of the Chan school. He who passes it not only sees Zhaozhou himself with his own eyes but may walk hand in hand, eyebrows locked together
(joined as one body)

, with the patriarchs of generation after generation, seeing with the same eye, hearing with the same ear — is that not joyful? Is there any who wishes to pass the barrier? Gather your three hundred and sixty bones, your eighty-four thousand pores, raise a ball of doubt throughout your body, contemplate the word 'wu,' and hold it on day and night. Do not take it as emptiness, do not take it as existence or non-existence. It is like swallowing a red-hot ball of iron: you try to spit it out but cannot. It cleanses away all former evil knowledge and evil perceptions. After a long, mature time, naturally inside and outside become one mass; like a dumb man's dream, it is known only to himself. Suddenly it breaks through — heaven-shaking, earth-moving; as though the great sword of the General Guan were seized in your hands, you slay the Buddha when you meet the Buddha, slay the patriarch when you meet the patriarch; at the brink of life and death you attain great freedom, and in the six destinies and four forms of birth you sport in samādhi. And how do you hold it
(then, how does one hold it?)
? Exert all your life's strength to raise the word 'wu'; if uninterrupted, it is like a dharma candle
(a candle)
— one touch, and it is lit."

[The Gateless Barrier (Wumen Guan)] The book the Gateless Barrier was compiled by the Song-dynasty Chan monk Wumen Huikai. Responding to the requests of students, he used the koans of the ancients as bricks with which to knock on the gate, leading them on as circumstances allowed; transcribing as he went along, before he knew it a collection had formed. The book contains forty-eight well-known koans of old, each followed by a verse and a comment. Its structure is first to present the case, then to add the comment, and finally to append his own verse. [The barrier of the patriarchs] The gate which the patriarchs must pass through; without passing this gate one cannot become a patriarch. The patriarchs' barrier is a state of sudden enlightenment, and the key to this gate lies in the single word 'wu'; only by penetrating it can one exhaust the path of the mind and attain wondrous awakening, walking hand in hand with the patriarchs of all generations. [Hold it (ti si)] To rouse and awaken oneself, keeping right mindfulness. Master Lianchi's Essentials of Buddha-Recollection says: 'May you let go of all conditions, and in the twelve hours hold it in thought at every moment — this is my earnest hope.' The Complete Works of Master Zhu

Cultivation and Nurture says: 'One need only constantly hold oneself to it, accumulating a bit at a time; after a long time it naturally connects and becomes one mass.' For instance, the Master Ruiyan would ask himself every day: 'Master, are you still awake?' And would answer himself: 'Awake, awake.' [Awake (xing xing)] Clear-minded. [Four forms of birth (si sheng)] Viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and spontaneously-born. [Dharma candle (fa zhu)] 'Candle,' the lamp of illumination. In the Han dynasty Liu An first made candles to replace oil lamps, and the Prince of Huainan widely promoted them, calling them 'dharma candles.'

Using the word 'wu' as the huatou, besides gathering ten thousand thoughts into one, the one returning to nothingness, until one sees the mind and realizes the nature, has another subtle virtue: the moment the word 'wu' is raised, one is instantly roused to watch against delusion, for originally there was not a single thing! Thus within, one does not follow the revolving thoughts, and without, one is not dragged along by circumstances. Master Hanshan says:

"If you cannot endure with patience and are obstructed by affliction, then as soon as you see it arise, raise the sentence of the Sixth Patriarch, 'originally there is not a single thing,' like the jeweled sword of the diamond king; then all affliction melts away in the present moment, and body and mind become a pool of cool clarity." (From the Dream Wanderings Collection

, Admonition to Xu Qingzhi) The Teaching of Vimalakirti says: "If a dharma is not received, it cannot be obtained; because it cannot be obtained, there is no grasping and no renouncing, no doing, no practicing — this is entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality"

[The Dharma-gate of non-duality] The teaching which transcends the relative and the differentiated and attains the absolute, equal truth of reality. The Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter nine, 'Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality,' sets forth thirty-three kinds of non-dual Dharma-gates. The Sutra Spoken by the Victorious One without Defilement, chapter nine, 'Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality,' says: 'Production and cessation are two; if the bodhisattvas know that all dharmas from the first neither arise nor cease, and realize this patient acceptance of the unproduced, this is entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.'

"The Sixth Patriarch's 'originally there is not a single thing' is what the Sixth Patriarch said: originally there is not a single thing. In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, Huineng's verse says: 'Bodhi has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand; originally there is not a single thing, where could dust alight?' 'Originally there is not a single thing' speaks of the true nature of all dharmas. In the Buddha-Store Sutra, the chapter on Buddha-Recollection, the Buddha says: 'What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are in the end empty, without anything at all.' The Buddha-Store Sutra, chapter one on the true nature of dharmas, says: 'All dharmas have no nature, empty, without anything.' In the Sutra of Upholding the World, chapter eighteen on the natures, the Buddha says: 'Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions with no reality, with no root.' In the Great Prajna Paramita Sutra, volume 341, the Buddha says: 'All dharmas are empty.'

'Originally there is not a single thing' is the contemplation of emptiness in the very substance of things. Body and mind, and the dust of the sense-realms, are all matters within the dream of ignorance; in their very substance they are empty. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: 'All sentient beings, from the beginningless past, have been in manifold inversion, like a confused man who changes his place in the four directions, wrongly taking the four great elements as his own body and the dependent image of the six sense-objects as his own mind. It is like a man with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon.' The Diamond Sutra says: 'All conditioned appearances are false and unreal. If you see that all appearances are not appearances, then you see the Tathagata.' Using this principle of sudden enlightenment ('originally there is not a single thing') as the power of contemplation, one breaks clinging and eradicates habits, and refines the mind through circumstances. It is like desiring to fell a poisonous tree: cut straight through its root, rather than seeking among its branches and plucking its leaves.
'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' This koan, besides being famous as a huatou, is itself profound in principle and highly instructive.
The Book of Equanimity says:
'A monk asked Zhaozhou: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?" Zhaozhou said: "It does." The monk said: "Since it does, why does it go and plunge into this leather bag
(this body)
?" Zhaozhou said: "Because it knows and yet deliberately offends
(because it knows, it deliberately commits this offense)

." Again a monk asked: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?" Zhaozhou said: "It does not." The monk said: "All sentient beings have Buddha-nature — why does the dog not?" Zhaozhou said: "Because it still has the active consciousness.""
Now let me analyze this koan as follows:
[A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said: 'It does.' The monk said: 'Since it has it, why does it go and plunge into this leather bag
(this body)
?' Zhaozhou said: 'Because it knows and yet deliberately offends.']

A monk asked the Chan master Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog also have Buddha-nature?' Zhaozhou answered: 'It does.' The monk went on: 'Since it has Buddha-nature, why does it still go and be reborn as a dog?' Zhaozhou answered: 'Because it stirs up thoughts, and so commits this error (running into this leather bag).'

The 'knows' in 'because it knows and yet deliberately offends' is the stirring of thoughts. Because sentient beings stir up thoughts, their original mind turns into a deluded mind; they arouse confusion and create karma, and revolve in the six destinies. Thus, though they have Buddha-nature, they follow the flowing active consciousness, slipping into donkey wombs and horse bellies, reaching everywhere. Although they slip into donkey wombs and horse bellies everywhere, the Buddha-nature is still present, only in an unmanifested state. Hence Zhaozhou said the dog has Buddha-nature.
[Again a monk asked: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said: 'No.']
Another monk asked: 'Does a dog also have Buddha-nature?' Zhaozhou answered: 'No.'

When Zhaozhou said 'No,' this word 'no' is the 'no' of 'originally there is not a single thing,' spoken with reference to the true reality of all dharmas. In terms of true reality, all dharmas do not exist, and the dog is naturally no exception. Since the dog itself does not exist, how can one speak of whether it has Buddha-nature? The 'nonexistence' one ordinarily speaks of is a negation in relation to existence, for instance, an ox has horns, a rabbit has none. This is a matter within the dream of ignorance. Practice is meant to illuminate the First Principle and break through the dream of ignorance. But these two monks did not understand the First Principle, and so continued circling within the dream of ignorance.

[The dream of ignorance] The Sutra of the Buddha's Inconceivable Realm says: 'All Tathagatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable great spiritual powers, and even enter into the emptiness of all dharmas (all dharmas are illusions), and are able to manifest all manner of sovereign deeds in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions. It is like a man who dreams of all sorts of transformation: when he awakes, none of what he saw exists. So too are ordinary beings: because of the dream of ignorance, they falsely conceive of real entities in all dharmas. The buddhas, having awakened, are attached to nothing, and thus can in a single thought manifest immeasurable buddha-deeds in all the worlds of the ten directions, freely and without obstruction, benefiting and perfecting all sentient beings, causing all of them to awaken into immeasurable, profound, and subtle gates of liberation.'
[The monk said: 'All sentient beings have Buddha-nature — why does the dog not?' Zhaozhou said: 'Because it still has the active consciousness.']
The monk retorted: 'All sentient beings have Buddha-nature — why has the dog no Buddha-nature?' Zhaozhou replied: 'Because it (and you) still has the active consciousness.'

Zhaozhou's answer is a double-edged sword: on the surface it says the dog, owing to its active consciousness, has its Buddha-nature latent; in fact it is reprimanding this monk: you are still sunk in the active consciousness, not understanding the First Principle, clinging to existence and nonexistence. Hence the Gateless Barrier's verse on this koan: 'The dog's Buddha-nature — the true command is raised in full; the moment you touch upon existence or nonexistence, you lose body and life (you lose the body of dharma-nature and the life of wisdom).' The master Fayan's verse says: 'Zhaozhou's naked sword, its cold frost flaring bright; you hesitate and ask, What is it? — he cuts your body into two.'

In 'because it still has the active consciousness,' the word 'yi' (it) is a personal pronoun. When used as a personal pronoun, 'yi' has two meanings. One is the third person, e.g., 'When I saw Zhang, he (yi) was already sixty.' (History of the Southern Dynasties). The other is the second person, equivalent to 'you,' e.g., 'Do not imitate your elder brother; your elder brother is not as good as he (yi).' (New Tales of the World, Worldly Sayings).

[The First Principle (diyi yidi)] The supremely exalted, perfect, and ultimate truth. The Buddha said: 'All dharmas are false and unreal; where they cease, that is called real, that is called the real mark, that is called the dharma-realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the First Principle, that is called the emptiness of the First Principle.' (The Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra) [The real mark (shixiang)] What is called 'real mark' is the actual circumstances; 'the real mark of all dharmas' is the actual circumstances of all dharmas. The Buddha-Store Sutra says: 'What is called the real mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are in the end empty, without anything at all.' The Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra says: 'All dharmas are like illusions; the Tathagata among them, by his power of expedient means, is attached to nothing.' The Lotus Sutra says: 'The bodhisattva mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, in accord with the real mark, without inversion, without agitation, without regression, without turning.' For a fuller discussion of the real mark of all dharmas, see our academy's textbook
Selected Annotations of the Buddha-Store Sutra

. [True command (zhengling)] The law and decree, referring to the Buddha-Dharma. In the Chan school it specifically refers to the purport transmitted apart from the teachings. The Book of Equanimity says: 'The tongueless man, the tongueless man, the true command raised in full in a single phrase is close.' [Transmitted apart from the teachings (jiaowa biezhuan)] 'Teachings' refers to the scriptures and doctrines, so 'transmitted apart from the teachings' is the special transmission outside them. The Five Lamps Merged in the Source, chapter on the World-Honoured One, says: 'The World-Honoured One, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a flower and showed it to the assembly. At that time, the millions of gods and humans were all at a loss (all without knowing what to do); alone the golden-robed elder (the elder Mahakashyapa) broke into a smile. The World-Honoured One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the real mark which is markless, the subtle Dharma-gate, not established in words, transmitted apart from the teachings — entrusted to the great Kashyapa (Mahakashyapa).'

That practitioners who do not understand the First Principle should cling to existence and nonexistence: there is a similar koan in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. The Platform Sutra records: When the Sixth Patriarch, having completed the Way, came out of the mountains and arrived at the Dharma-Nature Temple in Guangzhou, he happened upon the Dharma Master Yinzong expounding the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra.

"At that time the wind was blowing and the banner was moving. One monk said: 'The wind is moving.' Another monk said: 'The banner is moving.' They argued endlessly. Huineng advanced and said: 'It is not the wind moving, it is not the banner moving; it is the mind of the venerable one that is moving
(it is your minds that are moving)
. The whole assembly
(all the people)
were astounded
(greatly taken aback)
[Banner (fan)] A long, strip-shaped flag hung straight upright from a bamboo pole or the like.

When the wind moves the banner, it is not impermissible for the world's ordinary people to argue whether the wind moves or the banner moves, for they are already sunk in the dream of ignorance; but the practitioner, who is to awaken from the dream, should hold firmly to 'all conditioned appearances are false and unreal,' 'not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas,' guarding the original mind so that it is not turned by circumstances, and only then can one be free of birth and death. In the Shurangama Sutra the Buddha says: 'You should know that all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been continually born and dying, all because they do not know the ever-dwelling true mind, the pure and bright essence of nature, and use all sorts of vain imaginings; because these imaginings are not true, there is revolving.' So these two monks arguing there whether the wind or the banner moved is clinging to marks as real, the mind moving with circumstances, using vain imaginings — in truth not the conduct of one who practises. 'It is not the wind moving, it is not the banner moving' means that, from the standpoint of awakening, 'all conditioned appearances are false and unreal,' 'originally there is not a single thing' — how can there be any moving of wind or banner? And the words 'it is the mind of the venerable one that is moving (it is your minds that are moving)' strike at the very root: when the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind Ground says: 'All dharmas arise from vain imagining.' Master Hanshan's Record of the Lankavatara says: 'All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of false thought; if apart from thought, there are no marks of any realm.'

The Sixth Patriarch thus calmed this argument at the very root, which shows how high his state was (by 'high state' is meant not that he excelled in mysterious words and clever phrases, in a torrent of eloquence, but the practical power of unmoving suchness when root and dust meet), hence 'the whole assembly was astounded.' The words 'It is not the wind moving, it is not the banner moving; it is the mind of the venerable one that is moving' truly are earth-shattering! Sentient beings, amid the utterly still unborn, see only arising and ceasing; the buddhas, amid the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
